# The Query Language and Parser {#sec-query-language}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

NebulaStream speaks a SQL dialect that is close to standard SQL with
two extensions: a way to declare logical and physical sources
separately, and `INTO` clauses that route a query's output to a
named sink. The parser is built on ANTLR4. The binding step turns a
parse tree into a typed `LogicalPlan`. Both live in
`nes-sql-parser/`.

This chapter walks through the language and the parser. The
language is not fancy, but the source/sink declaration model
deserves a careful look — it is one of the more interesting design
choices in the engine.

---

## 5.1 The four DDL/DML shapes {#sec-shapes}

Every NebulaStream program is built from four kinds of statement.
We saw all four in our demo query in Chapter 2. Let us look at each
in isolation.

**Logical source.** Declares a named stream and its schema, with no
implementation:

```sql
CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE demo(value UINT64);
```

After this statement, `demo` is a name the rest of the program can
refer to, but nothing is producing data yet.

**Physical source.** Binds an implementation to a logical source:

```sql
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR demo
    TYPE File
    SET('./demo-input.csv' AS `SOURCE`.FILE_PATH,
        'CSV' AS PARSER.`TYPE`);
```

`TYPE` selects an implementation from the source registry. The
`SET(…)` clause carries arbitrary key-value configuration. The
backticks around `SOURCE` and `TYPE` are SQL-standard escaping for
identifiers that collide with reserved words.

**Sink.** Declares an output channel with a schema *and* an
implementation:

```sql
CREATE SINK result(demo.value UINT64)
    TYPE File
    SET('./demo-output.csv' AS `SINK`.FILE_PATH,
        'CSV' AS `SINK`.OUTPUT_FORMAT);
```

Note that sinks combine the logical declaration and the physical
implementation in one statement, unlike sources. We will see why in
@sec-source-vs-sink.

**Query.** A familiar `SELECT` with one twist: the output is named:

```sql
SELECT value FROM demo INTO result;
```

`INTO result` is required; NebulaStream queries always produce a
named output, never an anonymous result set. There is no client-
side cursor; if you want results in `nes-repl`, you declare a
`PrintSink` and route the query into it.

---

## 5.2 Why two source statements? {#sec-source-vs-sink}

The split between logical and physical source declarations is the
non-obvious part of the language. Most SQL engines combine the two:
`CREATE TABLE foo (x INT) ENGINE=File LOCATION='/path'` or its
moral equivalent. NebulaStream separates them. Why?

The reason is that one logical source can have *multiple* physical
sources, and the engine treats them as a single logical input. A
fleet of 200 vehicles can each have its own physical source —
perhaps an MQTT topic per vehicle — that all feed a single logical
source named `vehicles`. A query that reads from `vehicles` reads
from the union of all 200 physical sources, with the engine
managing parallelism, watermarks, and per-physical-source state
under the hood.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 5.1: a fleet of vehicles"}

```sql
CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE vehicles(
    id UINT64,
    speed FLOAT64,
    creationTS UINT64);

CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR vehicles TYPE TCP
    SET('vehicle-1.local' AS HOST, '5001' AS PORT, ...);
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR vehicles TYPE TCP
    SET('vehicle-2.local' AS HOST, '5001' AS PORT, ...);
-- ... 198 more ...
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR vehicles TYPE TCP
    SET('vehicle-200.local' AS HOST, '5001' AS PORT, ...);

SELECT id, speed FROM vehicles WHERE speed > 100 INTO alerts;
```

The `SELECT` is unaware of the 200-physical fan-in. The engine
treats `vehicles` as a single logical input whose physical
realisation happens to be 200 TCP connections. Adding or removing
a vehicle is a `CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE` or its inverse — no query
edit required.
:::

Sinks do not need this split because the analogous fan-out is
handled differently — typically by the application code that
consumes from the sink, not by the engine. A future direction may
introduce a logical/physical sink split if the symmetry becomes
useful; today it does not.

---

## 5.3 The grammar {#sec-grammar}

The grammar lives in `nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4`. Here is the
relevant slice:

```antlr
// nes-sql-parser/AntlrSQL.g4
createLogicalSourceDefinition:
    LOGICAL SOURCE sourceName=identifier schemaDefinition fromQuery?;

createPhysicalSourceDefinition:
    PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR logicalSource=identifier
    TYPE type=identifier
    optionsClause?;

createSinkDefinition:
    SINK sinkName=identifier schemaDefinition
    TYPE type=identifier optionsClause?;

optionsClause: (SET '(' options=namedConfigExpressionSeq ')');
```

Three observations.

First, the grammar is small. NebulaStream's SQL is intentionally a
subset of standard SQL; you will not find `WITH RECURSIVE`,
correlated subqueries, or PIVOT here. The streaming workloads the
engine targets simply do not need them.

Second, the grammar is unambiguous about `TYPE`. Both physical
source and sink declarations have a `TYPE` clause that selects the
implementation by name. The name must match an entry in the
source/sink registry (Chapter 13); unknown types produce a binding
error.

Third, the optional `fromQuery` on `createLogicalSourceDefinition`
hints at a feature the grammar supports: a logical source can be
defined as the result of a query over other sources. This is
NebulaStream's analogue of a materialised view. We will not cover
it in this chapter — it is a small slice — but it exists.

---

## 5.4 Statement binding {#sec-binding}

Parsing produces a tree of `AntlrSQLParser::*Context` nodes. Binding
turns that tree into a typed `LogicalPlan`. The binder lives in
`nes-sql-parser/src/StatementBinder.cpp`. Its contract is:

```cpp
// nes-sql-parser/src/StatementBinder.cpp
class StatementBinder::Impl {
    std::shared_ptr<const SourceCatalog> sourceCatalog;
    std::function<LogicalPlan(AntlrSQLParser::QueryContext*)> queryBinder;
public:
    using Literal = std::variant<std::string, int64_t, uint64_t, double, bool>;
    Impl(const std::shared_ptr<const SourceCatalog>& sourceCatalog,
         const std::function<LogicalPlan(AntlrSQLParser::QueryContext*)>&
             queryBinder)
        : sourceCatalog(sourceCatalog), queryBinder(queryBinder) {}
};
```

Binding does several things:

1. **Resolves names.** `demo` in `FROM demo` becomes a reference to
   the logical source registered under that name in the
   `SourceCatalog`. An unknown name is a `UnknownSourceType` error.
2. **Type-checks expressions.** A predicate like `WHERE speed >
   100` is checked: `speed` must be a numeric field, `100` is an
   integer literal, `>` is a binary operator with the right
   signature.
3. **Constructs operators.** Each clause in the query becomes a
   `LogicalOperator`. The DAG is assembled bottom-up: source nodes
   first, then projection/selection/window/join, then sink at the
   root.
4. **Validates output schemas.** The query's output schema must
   match the sink's declared schema. `SELECT value FROM demo INTO
   result` requires that `result`'s schema be compatible with the
   single-column projection.

The output is a `LogicalPlan` ready for the optimiser (Chapter 9).

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: SQL→AST→logical-plan in Calcite"}
Apache Calcite, the parser used by Flink SQL and Hive, follows a
similar shape: parse tree → SqlNode AST → RelNode logical plan,
with binding ("validation") in between. The two-stage approach is
ANTLR-style: keep the syntactic tree close to the grammar, do
semantic work in a second pass. NebulaStream's binder is much
simpler than Calcite's because the language is much smaller.
:::

---

## 5.5 The query catalog and source catalog {#sec-catalogs}

Two pieces of state outlive any single query: the `SourceCatalog`
and the `SinkCatalog`. Both live in
`nes-sources/include/Sources/SourceCatalog.hpp` and the analogous
sink path. They are simple key-to-descriptor maps.

When `CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE demo(value UINT64)` runs, the catalog
gets a new entry. When `CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR demo …` runs,
the catalog gets a physical descriptor attached to the existing
logical entry. When the user submits `SELECT … FROM demo`, the
binder looks up `demo` in the catalog to resolve the schema and
attach the physical descriptors.

Catalog entries persist across queries within a single worker
process. They do not (yet) persist across worker restarts. This is
a deliberate choice: NebulaStream is not, today, designed as a
metadata store.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch5-summary}

NebulaStream's SQL dialect uses four statement shapes: logical
source, physical source, sink, and query. The split between
logical and physical sources is the most distinctive feature: a
single logical source can have many physical realisations, and the
engine treats them as one fan-in stream. The grammar is small and
ANTLR4-based; binding produces a typed `LogicalPlan` from the
parse tree by resolving names against a `SourceCatalog`, type-
checking expressions, and assembling a DAG of `LogicalOperator`s.
There is no Calcite-scale validator; the language is small enough
for a straightforward visitor.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch5-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 5.1: parse a real query"}
Take the demo query from Chapter 2 and feed it to the standalone
parser test:

```shell
ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -R "AntlrSQLParserTest" \
    --output-on-failure
```

Open `nes-sql-parser/tests/` and find the test that parses a
similar four-statement script. Read the expected `LogicalPlan`
that the binder produces. How many operators? What is the
qualified field name of the sink's input?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 5.2: introduce a binding error"}
Modify the demo query so that the sink's schema does not match
the projection (e.g., declare `result(other UINT64)`). Submit it
and inspect the error. Where in `StatementBinder.cpp` is the
mismatch detected? Which exception code from
`nes-common/include/ExceptionDefinitions.inc` does it produce?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 5.3: extend the grammar"}
Suppose you wanted to add a `LIMIT N` clause to NebulaStream SQL.
Walk through the changes: a grammar rule in `AntlrSQL.g4`, a new
`LimitLogicalOperator` in `nes-logical-operators/`, a binding-step
addition in `StatementBinder.cpp`, an optimiser pass-through in
`nes-query-optimizer/`, a physical lowering in
`nes-physical-operators/`. You do not need to write the code; the
exercise is to identify every touchpoint.
:::
